title: Eiffel Tower, Paris, France
notes: Steel art. Tall, noticeable from any place in Paris, landmark and significant icon of the city. This Paris sunset holds a particular place in my travel voyages. Stitched strong to my memories, the sunset I witnessed sitting across the lawn in front of the tower, having few cold ones, beats any of my southern californian sunsets.
alt: Sunset at Eiffel Tower in Paris, France

title: Paris, France
notes: Straight up from underneath, through the plane trees. This is the same evening as the sunset frame — I spent most of that afternoon sitting across the lawn from the tower with a few cold ones, and then walked directly under it on the way out, which is when the scale of the thing actually lands. From this angle it stops being a landmark and goes back to being ironwork. That day is stitched strong into my memories.
alt: The Eiffel Tower from directly below, framed by plane trees

title: First Light
notes: Cadillac Mountain gave me the most beautiful sunrise of my life in 2017. Cadillac Mountain is one of the first places in USA to witness a sunrise. I woke up so insanely early and sat in the cold until that sun rose. It was beyond worth it. The anticipation of waking up early, feeling the morning chill sink into your bones as you wait, and the excitement of the horizon changing colors is like nothing else.
alt: Sunrise at Cadillac Mountain in Acadia National Park

title: Sunrise at Acadia National Park
notes: I have always loved a good sunrise and have often gone a long way out of my way to catch one. The sun clears the water, and then the birds turn up out of nowhere to get in the way of it, which is the part you can never plan for. Everything in the frame is either solid black or burning. Worth every early alarm it took to be standing there.
alt: The sun clearing the horizon over the Atlantic with birds in silhouette

title: Acadia National Park, Maine
notes: The same January morning at Otter Cliff, turned around to face the rock instead of the water. The spray had frozen solid onto the boulders along the bottom and the low sun was only catching the tops of the trees. I remember being completely miserable and completely happy at the same time, standing there waiting for the light to come round. That is most of what I go out for.
alt: Sunrise light on the coastal cliffs at Acadia National Park, Maine

title: Boston, Massachusetts
notes: Home ♥️♥️♥️ — Boston across the Charles, long exposure, the water gone completely to glass. Five years here, and they were the best years of my life. Two cities later it is still home, all of it.
alt: The Boston skyline at sunset across the Charles River

title: Otter Cliffs, Acadia National Park in Maine
notes: One of the coldest and finest sunrises I have witnessed so far. It was cold enough that the ocean itself was steaming — sea smoke, which comes up when the air sits so much colder than the water that the sea starts giving it off. My phone's battery died within a few minutes of me getting there. Two layers of jackets, hands going numb, trying to hold the camera steady long enough for one good frame. One hell of an adventure it was, and I am glad this one turned out to be a good one in the end.
alt: Sunrise over sea smoke off the coast at Acadia National Park, Maine

title: Thunder Hole, Acadia National Park
notes: Thunder Hole, where the stairs drop you down into a cut in the rock and the tide works away underneath. There is a small figure at the bottom of the rail if you look for it, and it is the only thing in the frame giving the drop any scale. The sky held that pink for maybe five minutes and then quit entirely. Maine in January asks a lot of you and then pays all of it back in about the time it takes to change a lens.
alt: The wooden stairs down into Thunder Hole at dusk, Acadia National Park, Maine

title: Boston Winters
notes: The Charles freezes over and the boats come out of the water to sit on the dock all winter, hulls up, waiting on a thaw that is still months away. Back Bay lit up across the ice, and the river gone quiet in a way it never is in summer. Blue hour, and cold enough that I had the whole dock to myself. Five Boston winters, and this is the version of them I still miss.
alt: Sailboats hauled onto a dock beside the frozen Charles River with the Back Bay skyline at dusk

title: Deer Island in Boston, Massachusetts
notes: Deer Island has been one of the places that is stitched in my core memory. I have always loved a good sunrise, and have often went distance to catch a good one. When I lived back in Boston, catching a good sunrise at Deer Island was one of the many favorite things I did frequently.
alt: Deer Island in Boston, Massachusetts

title: Parker River National Wildlife Refuge, Massachusetts
notes: Reeds going to silhouette against the last of the light at Parker River, out on the northeast coast of Massachusetts. The refuge matters enormously to migrating birds, and I spent a good part of my Boston years out there with a lens, waiting on something to happen. There is almost no wildlife in this frame at all. Sometimes you go out looking for birds and come back with the light instead, and those years handed me a lot of evenings like this one.
alt: Birding Adventure at Parker River National Wildlife Refuge, Massachusetts

title: Fenway Park, Boston
notes: Fenway is one of my favourite ballparks in the entire country. A panorama from the third base side, wide enough to take in the Wall and the grandstand together. Two things get everybody the first time: the Wall is shorter than it looks on television, and the whole park is far smaller than it has any right to be. But the reason I would go back any day of the week is the middle of the eighth, when the entire place stands up to sing Sweet Caroline. Thirty-odd thousand people who mostly cannot sing, doing it anyway, all at once.
alt: A panorama of Fenway Park during a day game

title: Charles River, Boston
notes: Same river, opposite season, shot from about a foot above the waterline. The skyline reads completely differently when you are sitting down in it instead of looking across from a bridge — everything gets taller and further away at the same time. Grey afternoon, flat water, and a long slow paddle back in. The Charles is the thread running through all five of those years.
alt: The bow of a kayak on the Charles River with the Boston skyline beyond

title: Yarmouth, Cape Cod
notes: Cape Cod is one of my favorite leisure destination. Every trip I've made to Cape Cod has always been memorable. The sunsets at Gray's Beach at Yarmouth are one the most spectacular events I have witnessed while living on East Coast. Definitely a hidden Cape Cod gem.
alt: Gray's Beach at Yarmouth in Cape Cod, Massachusetts

title: Cape Cod, Atlantic Ocean
notes: The marsh turns gold a good while before the sky does, and for twenty minutes or so the grass is the brightest thing out there. People were still on the boardwalk waiting for the rest of it to happen. Low tide, no wind, the water sitting in the channels holding all of the light. The sunsets down here are some of the most spectacular things I witnessed in all my years on the East Coast.
alt: A boardwalk over the marsh at sunset on Cape Cod

title: Cape Cod Sunsets
notes: The same boardwalk, shot down the length of the rail instead of across it. The sky was doing enough work on its own that I did not want anything else competing in the frame. These are the last few minutes before the whole thing goes flat, and I have never worked out how to stop chasing them.
alt: Boardwalk railing against an orange sunset over the Cape Cod marsh

title: Cape Cod, Massachusetts
notes: The Sandwich boardwalk, which starts more or less nowhere, runs out over the marsh, and delivers you onto a beach with dunes and nesting grounds at the far end. Look down as you walk and every plank has a name cut into it — families, birthdays, people being remembered. It is the only boardwalk I know where the floor is worth as much attention as the view.
alt: Cape Cod, Massachusetts

title: Cape Cod
notes: Cape Cod is one of my favourite places on this coast and every trip I have made down there has been memorable. A rolled path laid over the dunes, two people already at the far end of it and into the water. The dunes sit high enough that you cannot see the ocean at all until you are right on top of it, and then it opens up all at once. That walk out, where the sound reaches you before the view does, is the part I keep going back for.
alt: A matted path over the dunes down to the water on Cape Cod

title: Seattle, Washington
notes: Seattle happened by chance. I got enough out of Boston, got myself a new job in the city, which made me pack my bags and make the big move across the country. Seattle has a reputation of being gloomy, which is true for the most part. Nevertheless, the new home has a lot to offer and I've started liking it. To the new beginnings...
alt: Seattle, Washington

title: Public Market of Seattle, Washington
notes: The first thing I had to see when I started shooting Seattle was the Public Market. It is a working market that happens to double as a tourist attraction, which is a harder balance to strike than it sounds — food and flower stalls, the catch of the day going over the counter in the fish market, and nine million visitors a year moving through the middle of it. Masks were still required the day I went. I came for the sign and stayed about three hours, and I have gone back more times than I can count since.
alt: Public Market of Seattle, Washington

title: Pike Place Market of Seattle, Washington
notes: The clock and the sign from underneath, with the market in full flow beneath it — umbrellas out, every bench taken, people eating standing up because there is nowhere left to sit. Most photographs of this place are taken from across the street with the whole sign in frame. I like this angle better. You lose half the letters and you gain the actual market.
alt: Pike Place Market of Seattle, Washington

title: Flower Stalls, Pike Place Market, Seattle, Washington
notes: If you get to Pike Place early enough, the flower stalls are still at full capacity and nothing has been picked over yet. Dahlias, gladiolus, whatever came in that morning, wrapped in paper and priced at something that feels like a mistake. Fresh enough and cheap enough that you walk out wanting to buy a bunch for everyone you know.
alt: Flower Stalls, Pike Place Market, Seattle, Washington

title: First Starbucks, Seattle, Washington
notes: The original Starbucks, near the waterfront end of Pike Place, still showing that modest old sign. The line runs out the door and down the block, the coffee is identical to every other Starbucks on earth, and you go anyway — because this is the room where it started. I stood in that line fully aware of how silly it was and enjoyed every minute of it.
alt: Original Starbucks in Seattle

title: Mount Baker Highway, Washington
notes: Straight down onto the highway from above. The forest closes in so completely on both sides that the road ends up being the only thing in the frame with a hard edge to it, and everything else reads as texture. One car, which is the only reason any of this has a sense of scale. That whole summer I was driving these roads trying to catch every PNW mountain I could, and somewhere along the way the drives themselves became the thing worth stopping for.
alt: An aerial view straight down onto a road cutting through dense conifer forest in Washington

title: Cape Flattery, Washington
notes: The furthest northwest tip of the contiguous United States, and on my list well before I ever moved to the PNW. The drive out is genuinely absurd. Then the trail starts in deep forest, turns into an easy boardwalk, and a few minutes later drops you onto a coastline with 180 degrees of Pacific in front of you and nothing beyond it. That is the whole country running out under your feet, and it is worth every hour of the drive.
alt: Cape Flattery, Washington

title: Mount Rainier, Washington
notes: Washington weather means you rarely get to see Rainier at all, let alone like this. I had been chasing this mountain since I moved to the PNW and had several drives end in cloud with nothing to show for them. This was the one that finally paid out — the whole thing standing clear, fourteen thousand feet of it, and no haze anywhere. Every failed attempt was worth it for this.
alt: Mount Rainier, Washington

title: Reflection Lake, Mount Rainier, Washington
notes: Reflection Lake, doing exactly what it is named for. Come early or come late, when the water has gone completely still, and the mountain arrives twice. I stood there long enough for the surface to settle and the reflection to sharpen up, and it remains one of the few places I have been where the photograph is essentially handed to you.
alt: Mount Rainier, Washington State

title: Picture Lake, Washington
notes: Picture Lake is the most incredible sight I've seen in the entire of Washington. Located in Northern Washington, Picture Lake is about a 3 hour drive from Seattle. With Mount Shuksan in the background and the wildflowers in the foreground, Picture lake is, well, as pretty as, a post card picture. The location is almost always full of people. I had to wait for 30 minutes for the people to clear up the space before I could capture it.
alt: Picture Lake, Washington

title: Mount Baker, Washington
notes: Mount Baker is a 10,781 ft active glacier-covered andesitic stratovolcano in the Cascade Volcanic Arc and the North Cascades of Washington. This was one of the bucketlist in my attempt to capture all the PNW mountains. The drive is long and crooked, but it was so worth it. Witnessing the sun setting down, and the mountain shining bright, I forgot all my miseries.
alt: Mount Baker, Washington

title: Mount Shuksan, Washington
notes: Another day, another bucketlist Mountain. Right at the Artist Point, Mount Shuksan is one of North America’s most iconic peaks. Situated on the western flank of the rugged North Cascades National Park, the mountain is capped by glaciers and surrounded by picturesque alpine lakes and meadows. Seeing that glacier up so close, and witnessing the sun rays falling all over it, it dazzles you right at the first sight. Mount Shuksan is my most favorite mountain in PNW.
alt: Mount Shuksan, Washington

title: Public Market, Seattle
notes: The Public Market sign from round the back, a construction crane parked behind it and Elliott Bay gone completely flat and grey. One man walking past underneath, not looking up at any of it. Seattle has a reputation for being gloomy and it is true for the most part — this is the version of the market that nobody photographs. By this point I had stopped waiting on the weather to improve and started shooting it as it came.
alt: The Public Market sign in Seattle seen against a construction crane and Elliott Bay on a grey day

title: Rains on Pike Place Market, Seattle
notes: The neon works harder in the wet. Rain had the cobbles holding all the red off the sign, and everyone was crossing quickly with their heads down, which is the correct way to move through Seattle in February. Nobody stops for the sign once they live here. I still did, occasionally.
alt: Pedestrians crossing wet cobblestones under the Public Market Center sign in the rain, Seattle

title: San Francisco Pier
notes: Pier 7, looking back down the length of it at the Transamerica Pyramid, benches and lampposts running away on both sides. This was not long after I landed in San Francisco. I had studied in southern California years before, so the state itself was not new, but this end of it was. Third city in a decade, and I spent those first few weeks doing what I always do — walking it with a camera until it started to make sense.
alt: San Francisco, California

title: California Street, San Francisco
notes: San Francisco lines itself up for you if you stand in the right place. California Street from up on Nob Hill, cable car tracks running straight down the middle and the Bay Bridge sitting at the end of them. A long lens stacks it all together and flattens the hill out of the picture entirely — in person you are looking down a very steep slope. Half the street was already in shadow and the other half was lit like it had been staged. A few months in, and the city was still surprising me every time I got above street level.
alt: Looking east down California Street toward the Bay Bridge from Nob Hill, San Francisco

title: Baker Beach, San Francisco
notes: You can see the Golden Gate from most of this city, but Baker Beach is where you get the whole span at once, with the headlands stacked up behind it and a stretch of sand to wait on while the light comes around. Someone had pitched a small tent near the waterline. Someone else was standing ankle deep in the surf with their back to all of it. Neither of them looked at the bridge once the entire time I was there, which is what living somewhere eventually does to a landmark. I had been here six months and had not got there yet.
alt: The Golden Gate Bridge at golden hour seen from Baker Beach, San Francisco

title: Stinson Beach, California
notes: Stinson Beach, an hour north of the city if the road over Mount Tamalpais treats you well. The fog had caught on the ridge behind the beach and the sun was coming through it sideways, which turned everything gold and pressed the hills flat into layers. The old fence posts were already there, running down toward the water, and all I really did was line up behind them. Most of the photographs I like best are like that — the composition was already sitting there and my only job was to not get in its way.
alt: Fence posts along Stinson Beach at sunset with a fog-covered ridge behind

title: Sunset at Stinson Beach
notes: Two minutes after the last frame. The sun dropped just far enough to take everyone down to silhouette — the pair standing by the posts, two more walking the waterline further along. Once the faces go you stop reading it as people and start reading it as shapes on a beach. That is usually the point where I put the camera down and just watch, and it is usually the frame I end up keeping.
alt: Silhouetted figures on Stinson Beach under a golden sunset

title: Mount Tamalpais, California
notes: Ridgecrest Boulevard on Mount Tamalpais in late August, with the entire Pacific buried under fog. You climb up through the grey for twenty minutes and then all at once you are above it, the fog sitting flat to the horizon like someone put a lid on the ocean. The grass had gone completely gold, the way it does out here by then. A single car came around the bend while I was set up, which was lucky, because without it there is nothing in the frame to tell you how big any of this is. I spent two years in Washington driving at mountains, and that habit came south with me.
alt: A car on Ridgecrest Boulevard above the fog layer on Mount Tamalpais, Marin County, California

title: Half Dome, Yosemite National Park
notes: You come around the bend, the pines part, and Half Dome is just there, framed for you, with a double yellow line running your eye straight into it. I had been looking at that rock all day from other angles, but this is the version you actually see first — through a windshield, from a road. Every photograph of this thing is one somebody has already taken, which stopped bothering me a long time ago. You do not pull over for an original angle. You pull over because it is Half Dome.
alt: Half Dome framed by pines above a curving road in Yosemite National Park, California

title: Tokyo Metro, Japan
notes: Tokyo had been on my bucket list for years and I finally got there sideways — a layover on the way to India that I stretched out into four days and three nights. I went for all of it: the food, the architecture, the culture, the whole way of life that everybody online will not stop talking about. This is an ordinary weekday platform. Everyone lined up exactly where the doors were going to open, nobody drifting, nobody jockeying for position. I dragged the shutter to let the train blur through and keep the people still, which is close to how the city actually feels — moving very fast around a set of very calm rules.
alt: Commuters waiting on a Tokyo Metro platform as a train blurs past

title: Nakamise-dori, Asakusa, Tokyo
notes: Nakamise-dori, the street that runs from the Kaminarimon up to the Hozomon gate at Senso-ji. It has been a market street for something like three hundred years and it is still doing exactly the same job: snacks, souvenirs, paper fortunes, and a great deal of foot traffic. I shot it long so the whole street compresses down into the gate at the end of it. Three centuries of feeding people, and it earned every one of the several trips I made back to it.
alt: Nakamise-dori shopping street leading to the Hozomon gate at Senso-ji, Asakusa, Tokyo

title: Five-Storied Pagoda, Senso-ji, Tokyo
notes: Senso-ji's pagoda, shot from inside a doorway on the far side of the courtyard. A good part of why I came to Tokyo was the architecture, and this is the reason why — the building I was standing in framed the one I was photographing, and I did not have to do anything clever about it. December had stripped the tree beside it back to bare branches except for one ginkgo that had not let go yet, about the only colour in the scene that was not red, grey or timber. Frames like this are mostly patience: you find the opening, then wait for the courtyard to hand you a second where nobody is standing in it.
alt: The five-storied pagoda at Senso-ji framed through a temple doorway, Asakusa, Tokyo

title: Hozomon Gate, Senso-ji, Tokyo
notes: The Hozomon gate with the big lantern hanging underneath it and New Year decorations strung out overhead. Cold, bright, and completely packed, which as far as I could tell is the normal state of Asakusa at more or less any hour. I gave up waiting for a gap in the crowd about ten minutes in and decided the crowd was the point. The life of the place was half of what I had come for.
alt: The Hozomon gate and New Year decorations above Nakamise-dori, Asakusa, Tokyo

title: Sushi Counter, Tokyo
notes: Ten seats at most, one chef working directly in front of you with nothing between the two of you but the case. Family crests tiled across the wall behind him, an old terracotta floor, and the whole room about the width of a hallway. Rooms like this one were the entire reason I detoured through Tokyo. Not the landmarks — small places doing a single thing carefully for a very long time. Four days was nowhere near enough.
alt: A chef at work behind a small sushi counter in Tokyo
